role: Junior 3D / Rendering Developer at a Digital Twin Company
headline: Fresh out of a bachelor's in automation and hired by a digital twin company in Wuhan's Optics Valley: a junior 3D developer who spends the day in Unity cutting polygons and lighting a car assembly hall, and every few days gets pulled off to tune the giant screen in a district command center
unit: A tech company in Wuhan's Optics Valley that builds digital twins of factories, industrial parks and city districts
unit_type: Private software company (about two hundred staff)
level: You built two small projects in C# and Unity at school, and you learned how PLCs and sensors work in class. But a single BIM model from a design institute can freeze your graphics card, you can't yet read an OPC UA tag list, and for light baking you rely on tutorials.
intro: You studied automation in Wuhan, and during a senior-year internship at a company in Optics Valley you saw, for the first time, a screen dozens of meters long in a command hall, with factories and streets moving across it. After graduation you signed with this company, your desk on the ninth floor of a building in Software New Town. As of today you start by cutting polygons and setting lights, learning to make what's on the screen move together with what's real outside.
salary_note: Estimate: digital twin companies in Optics Valley pay new graduates a little below the national average (the database figures come mostly from Shanghai and Shenzhen job ads), with an allowance for on-site work. In years when clients pay slowly, bonuses and raises get pushed back.

facts.label: Junior Digital Twin 3D / Rendering Developer (current level)
facts.value: 0-2 years, ¥8,500–9,500 a month (national average, estimated from pay by experience)

facts.label: Next level up
facts.value: Digital Twin Engineer / Unity3D Digital Twin Engineer (2-4 years)

facts.label: What AI can't take
facts.value: Installing the big screen in a command hall and getting it through acceptance

facts.label: Where AI is moving in
facts.value: Slimming a client's BIM model until it runs smoothly in a browser

facts.label: Open positions
facts.value: 0 related listings nationwide, 0 in this city (mostly campus hiring and internships)

day: Below your rented room in Guanshan you buy a bowl of hot dry noodles, eat as you walk, and squeeze onto the bus to Software New Town. Outside the window, each Optics Valley tower is newer than the last.

You open Unity. The assembly hall BIM model from the design institute has more than eight million faces, and the scene stutters whenever you drag it. You pull it into Blender and delete it bolt by bolt until it can spin in a browser.

The project manager comes over: next Tuesday district officials are coming to the command center to see the city screen, so smooth out the aerial fly-over a bit more. You nod and push the rest of today's plan back half a day.

You go with Peng, an implementation engineer, to a carmaker's final assembly hall out in the auto district, standing in a hard hat beside the AGV lane. He points at a nutrunner: this tool's torque data goes over OPC UA. You write the tags into your sheet one by one.

A process engineer on the floor asks why the AGV on the screen lags half a beat behind the real one. You say the data refreshes once a second. He says what they need is to see which one is stuck, not to watch it move nicely.
Back at the office an artist has swapped in a new car-body material, and you spend ages on the lighting; the floor of the paint shop keeps looking like a puddle.
You leave the light bake running on your machine all night, the GPU fan roaring. Before going you stick a note on your desk: do not shut down.
On the way home you have barbecue by Optics Valley Square. Peng sends a tag sheet to your phone with a line after it: see you at the hall gate at eight tomorrow.

ladder.title: Junior Digital Twin 3D / Rendering Developer
ladder.focus: Build 3D scenes, debug rendering, organize model assets and help deliver visualization features. You move up by learning the engine and data integration.

ladder.title: Digital Twin Engineer / Unity3D Digital Twin Engineer
ladder.focus: Handle data integration, platform setup and on-site implementation and debugging on your own, owning anything from one module to a whole project.

ladder.title: Digital Twin Simulation Engineer / Senior Digital Twin Engineer
ladder.focus: Do simulation modeling, virtual-to-physical mapping and predictive analysis; pay runs higher in automotive and autonomous driving.

ladder.title: Digital Twin Project Manager / Solutions Architect
ladder.focus: Own the overall solution, the team and delivery, and work with clients on what the industry needs.

ladder.title: Digital Twin Technical Expert / Head of R&D
ladder.focus: Top R&D roles such as industrial digital twins, defining the platform's technical direction.

ai_tasks.name: Slimming a client's BIM model until it runs smoothly in a browser
ai_tasks.how: AI and automation tools can batch-convert formats, reduce polygons and compress textures, and write scripts to chain the steps. A person has to decide which key components and what precision to keep, check that nothing went missing or shifted after decimation, and agree with the client on what looks acceptable.

ai_tasks.name: Running a requirements study and producing a data-source list
ai_tasks.how: AI can tidy interview notes, generate a study outline and a data-source template, and merge duplicates. A person has to go see the park or factory, work out what the client really wants, which data can actually be had and who is willing to open it up. That part is communication and judgment.

ai_tasks.name: Installing the big screen in a command hall and getting it through acceptance
ai_tasks.how: AI can help draft the deployment checklist and the demo script. But installing hardware in the client's command hall, setting resolutions, handling every hardware and network surprise, walking the client through acceptance and getting their signature all need a person there, answering for it.

ai_tasks.name: Bringing a production line's sensor data into the twin and wiring up alarms
ai_tasks.how: AI can draft the integration code, field mappings and alarm rules, and help track down interface errors. A person has to agree protocols and tags with the line and the equipment vendor, set sensible alarm thresholds, test that the linkage is reliable, and answer for false and missed alarms.

ai_tasks.name: Recovering on site when the big screen suddenly drops frames before a demo
ai_tasks.how: AI can help read logs, analyze performance metrics and suggest likely causes. But within half an hour someone on site has to judge whether it's rendering, data or network, change configurations, swap hardware or fall back to a simpler plan, and keep things steady in front of the client. It comes down to experience and decisions in the moment.

ai_tasks.name: Building a simulation model of a production line and validating the virtual-physical mapping
ai_tasks.how: AI can help scaffold the simulation model, clean data, run parameter fitting and propose optimizations. A person has to understand the process, decide how far to simplify the model, calibrate it against real data, judge whether virtual and real agree, and explain to the client whether the conclusions can be trusted.

ai_tasks.name: Taking over quarterly operations and upgrades for a delivered platform
ai_tasks.how: AI can handle routine checks, data-refresh scripts, alert sorting and keeping docs and change logs. A person has to set the direction and priorities for upgrades, guard security and permissions, handle production incidents, and talk to the client about costs and changing needs.

events.e_demo_lag: The night before a demo, the command hall screen drops frames every time it cuts to the city panorama. You dig on site until two in the morning: a stretch of river with a transparent material that keeps stacking on itself. You swap the shader, and the next day the officials' tour runs smoothly.
events.e_flyover: On the day of the officials' visit, what gets the most praise is the aerial fly-over you spent a week tuning. Nobody asks about the three months of live data you integrated. On the way back the project manager says: first make people understand it, then make them use it.
events.e_summer: July in Wuhan, thirty-nine degrees, and you are on site tuning sensors in the stamping shop, with no air conditioning, only a few big fans. After a week your back is covered in prickly heat and you have drunk dozens of bottles of iced mung bean soup.
events.e_rain: In the plum-rain season a heavy storm hits, and the district command center actually uses your waterlogging module for the first time. Red dots light up one by one on the screen where the water at an intersection is over twenty centimeters, and the emergency trucks head where they point.
events.e_ai_mesh: A new optimization tool can automatically decimate a whole building's BIM and compress its textures. Work that used to take you two weeks now finishes in an afternoon. Your time goes instead to checking component by component: the fire sprinkler pipes are still there, the stairs haven't shifted.
events.e_ai_code: AI can now write seventy or eighty percent of the data-integration code, with first drafts of the field mappings and alarm rules thrown in. Checking it line by line against the on-site tag sheet, you find it has swapped the tags for two cooling pumps.
events.e_false_alarm: A temperature alarm you brought into the twin fires falsely more than forty times in a week, and the shop director says in the group chat that if it goes off again he'll switch it off. You trace it to a sensor range set wrong on site, after spending three days adjusting the alarm threshold.
events.e_payment: A year after acceptance, a city platform company still hasn't paid for a project. Cash is tight and salaries are two months late. At an all-hands the boss says everyone will be paid. You borrow those two months' rent from your roommate.
events.e_bid_win: Bidding for a city-wide twin platform, your team pulls three all-nighters building the demo. On the day the bids are opened you wait at the office, and when the award notice lands in the group chat, everyone goes out together for crayfish.
events.e_bid_lose: A bid you led loses to a big tech company that quoted half your price. Later you go look at the system they delivered. The camera work really is beautiful, and the data they connected is a third of what your plan had.
events.e_steel: You go to a steelworks in Qingshan to build a twin of a blast furnace, and one night you watch a tapping: molten iron pours from the taphole like a bright orange river. Back at your computer, you redo the colors of that section of the screen three times.
events.e_bridge: On the structural health twin you built for a bridge over the Yangtze, one night the vibration data on a single hanger cable stays high, and the alarm goes to the maintenance authority. The next day someone climbs up to check: a damper has come loose.
events.e_game: Your college roommate builds scenes at a game studio in Optics Valley, earning a good deal more than you, and posts the graphics card he won in the company's year-end raffle. You give it a like and go back to texturing a model of a septic tank.
events.e_eyes: Your eyes are so dry that they water after a few minutes at the screen. The doctor says it's dry eye and tells you to look into the distance every twenty minutes. You tape a photo of East Lake beside your monitor as a reminder.
events.e_cert: You pass the intermediate certificate for industrial internet engineering technicians. The practical exam is connecting a simulated device's data to a platform and setting up alarms, and you finish in half the time.
events.e_wedding: You get married, to someone who does quality inspection at an optical module plant in Optics Valley. The wedding is back home in Xiangyang, and you make a little 3D animation of the wedding car route that the relatives pass around.
events.e_house: You buy an apartment in Baoxie, on the east side of Optics Valley, with a down payment pooled from both sets of parents and your own savings. On signing day you stand a long time in front of the model in the sales office, thinking it isn't very accurate.
events.e_child: Your child is born. You take ten days of paternity leave, and on day eleven you're called into the command center to tune the screen. At lunch you squeeze in a video call, and the baby is crying.
events.e_old_platform: A business park twin you delivered five years ago is still in use. On the annual maintenance visit you notice the lawn texture on the big screen is still the one you hand-tuned tile by tile years ago. One patch is a little darker, and no one has ever noticed.
events.e_autodrive: Autonomous driving testing in the auto district gets hotter every year, and your company takes a job on a simulated intersection: moving a real stretch of street, its traffic lights and its pedestrians into simulation, so the cars can drive it tens of thousands of times first.
events.e_auto_twin: Now a drone flies one loop, and AI generates a twin of the whole park by itself, streetlights and all. Your work becomes checking item by item: which data is truly connected, and which is only for looks.
events.e_back: Years of sitting, and your lower back starts to protest. You buy an expensive chair, and start walking an hour along the East Lake greenway after work every day.

c_onsite.title: Six months on site in the auto district
c_onsite.situation: The carmaker's assembly hall project needs someone on site for six months, matching tags with Peng, installing gateways and tuning things alongside the shop. There's an on-site allowance, but you'd have to be in the hall by seven every morning and leave when the line does. Back at the office you'd keep doing rendering, and your scenes would keep getting prettier.

options.label: Go on site
options.result: In six months you learn to read electrical drawings and to speak the same language as the shop electricians. The first thing you do back at the office is delete the decorative lights in your scene that don't exist anywhere in the real hall.

options.label: Stay at the office and render
options.result: You turn the riverside view on the city screen into the company's signature showcase; sales plays it first at every client meeting. But when the hall calls with a data question, you still have to pass it to someone else.

c_data.title: Learn data integration and go for Digital Twin Engineer
c_data.situation: Your lead says that to become a Digital Twin Engineer and own a module, making scenes isn't enough: you have to be able to bring the equipment data in yourself. MQTT, OPC UA, time-series databases, all of it. It means spending evenings and weekends on a heap of things that have nothing to do with pictures.

options.label: Dig in
options.result: In your rented room you simulate a device on a dev board and run its temperature data from the sensor all the way to a little light in the 3D scene. The first time the light turns red with the warmth of your finger, you laugh out loud, alone.

options.label: Make the visuals the best first
options.result: You become the company's best lighter; even the artists come to ask you. The data side goes to someone else and the two of you work well together, though in the project report the module owner listed is him.

c_shanghai.title: Shanghai makes a big offer
c_shanghai.situation: A large smart-factory company in Shanghai is hiring digital twin engineers at one and a half times your current pay, on projects for big carmakers and chip fabs. But your parents are in Xiangyang, your partner is in Wuhan, and Shanghai rent would eat half the salary.

options.label: Go to Shanghai
options.result: On a Shanghai project you see a production line with thousands of tags for the first time, and every standard, process and review in place. On weekends you walk the Bund alone, then go back to your rented room and keep revising the plan.

options.label: Stay in Wuhan
options.result: You turn it down. On weekends you cycle around East Lake with your partner, and on Monday you're at the command center as usual. Your Wuhan projects are smaller, but every one of them is yours from start to finish.

c_sim.title: Move into simulation and go for Digital Twin Simulation Engineer
c_sim.situation: The company has won a virtual commissioning job in the auto district: before the line is installed, run every robot, conveyor and cycle time through the computer first. It needs someone who can build simulation models and virtual-physical mappings, and whoever does it becomes the company's first Digital Twin Simulation Engineer. But you'd have to learn process engineering and math from the ground up.

options.label: Take it on and learn the process and the math
options.result: You copy the line's cycle-time sheet across a whole wall. The bottleneck station your simulation finds is exactly where the real line jams three months later when it starts production. For the first time the shop director calls you himself.

options.label: Stay in implementation
options.result: Simulation goes to a master's graduate hired from a university, and you keep doing implementation and screens. Your reputation on site keeps growing, and clients start asking for you by name.

c_ai.title: Should you take charge of the AI delivery process?
c_ai.situation: More and more models, code and configurations come from AI first, and the company wants someone to set the rules: what can be used as is, what needs human checking, how prompts are written, how errors are traced. There are no existing targets for this work; do it well and nobody notices, do it badly and it's all on you.

options.label: Take it and set the rules
options.result: You write a twenty-page delivery standard that spells out, at each step, what AI produces, what a person checks and who signs. New implementation engineers follow it, and rework on their first project is cut in half.

options.label: Decline and keep doing projects
options.result: You say you still like being on site. Someone from the technical department writes the standard later; you read it and add three pitfalls in the group chat that only someone on site would know.

c_bim.title: A design institute wants you for BIM
c_bim.situation: A big design institute in Wuhan is hiring BIM engineers and likes that you know model optimization and engines. The institute is stable, with a housing fund and an annuity, no on-site stints and no all-nighters fixing screens. But the work is building models; you'd no longer connect equipment data or deal with factories.

options.label: Go to the design institute
options.result: You leave your on-site hard hat to a new colleague, the brim still stained with oil from the shop floor.
options.end: You do BIM at the institute for many years and later lead a small team, seeing building after building from drawings into models. Now and then, passing the auto district, you think of that AGV that always ran half a beat behind the real one.

options.label: Stay in digital twins
options.result: You turn the institute down. That month your job is a sewage treatment plant: it stinks, but the data is the most complete you've ever had, and you connect every single pump.

c_pm.title: Apply for Digital Twin Project Manager / Solutions Architect
c_pm.situation: The company is promoting someone to Digital Twin Project Manager / Solutions Architect, running everything from bid to design to delivery, leading a dozen people, presenting to clients' department directors and plant managers. You'd write less code, drink more at dinners, travel more, and chase payments yourself.

options.label: Apply
options.result: When you present, you don't open with the aerial fly-over. You open with a data-source list: this can be connected, this can't be had. The senior executive on the panel nods.

options.label: Stay on the technical track
options.result: You recommend a colleague who came up through sales and stay on the hardest sites yourself. Your desk holds hard hats from several projects, each older than the last.

c_expert.title: Go for Digital Twin Technical Expert / Head of R&D
c_expert.situation: The company wants a Digital Twin Technical Expert / Head of R&D to set the technical direction for the next-generation platform: which engine, how AI should generate scenes, how the data foundation should be built. It means many meetings with the boss, investors and several big clients' technical heads, and answering for success or failure years down the line.

options.label: Apply and write the roadmap
options.result: The first page of your roadmap has one sentence: pretty scenes aren't worth money anymore; data that actually connects is. The boss prints it out and pins it up in the meeting room.

options.label: Keep leading projects
options.result: You don't apply, and keep taking a delivery team out to sites. In one year you deliver six projects, all of them fully paid, and the boss raises a glass to you at the year-end party.

c_own.title: Open a studio of your own
c_own.situation: Over the years you've seen so many small factories in counties and development zones that want a screen showing their own equipment but can't pay big-company prices. Peng says he wants out too: the two of you could open a studio doing small twins for small plants, cheap, fast and usable. No salary, just one job after another.

options.label: Go out on your own
options.result: On the day you resign, you peel the East Lake photo off your desk and tuck it into your notebook.
options.end: Your studio with Peng is in an old building in Optics Valley, making twins for small plants in Ezhou, Xiaogan and Xiantao, a few tens of thousands of yuan a job, delivered fast. Every year you go back to visit, standing on the shop floor watching the little lights on the screen come on together with the real machines.

options.label: Stay
options.result: You help Peng land his first job but stay put yourself. He often sends photos afterward, always of a little screen in some county-town workshop.

endings.retire: On your last day you go to the command center once more. The big screen has been replaced twice; the city on it is far more detailed than it was, even the boats on the river move. You stand at the back and watch for a while, and no one recognizes you. When you step outside it's dark, and the real city is lighting up, one window at a time.
endings.burnout: That year your eyes and your back give out together, and the doctor says you can't keep sitting up nights in front of screens. You resign and rest at home for a year, spending your days sitting by East Lake watching the water. The computer at home is rarely on, and when it is, it's only to see whether the waterlogging module still lights up on rainy days.

stages: Your days are 3D scenes: pulling BIM and CAD models into Blender to decimate them and convert them to glTF, placing lights, tuning materials and scripting camera moves and click interactions in Unity. Implementation engineers bring tag sheets back from site, and you match every piece of equipment in the scene to its number. Comments from artists, the project manager and the client all land on you first; your job is to change things, not to decide them.

You own anything from a module to a whole project: on site you agree protocols and tags with equipment vendors, bring the data into a time-series database over MQTT and OPC UA, and wire it to alarms in the scene. You're the one who has to line up the client's electricians, the plant's IT office and your own artists and back-end team, and for the first time your name is on the acceptance form.

Your job is no longer just to make the screen move with the site, but to run the site in the computer first: building simulation models, calibrating the virtual-physical mapping, predicting which machine will fail and which station will jam. You sit in reviews with the plant's process engineers, university researchers and the client's technical section chief, and you have to explain why a prediction can be trusted, and how far.

You run the whole business: bids, solutions, schedules, a dozen people's assignments, and collecting payment. By day you meet clients' department directors and plant managers and translate what they say they want into a data-source list; at night you check your team's progress sheets and go argue scope changes with clients on their behalf. You write little code now, and sign more and more contracts.

You decide how the company's next-generation platform will be built: which engine, how the data foundation is laid, how AI-generated scenes are governed. You meet the boss, investors and several big clients' technical heads, review every project team's technical plans and sign the key architecture review forms. You go to sites less often, and each time it's to see the hardest one.
work: The factory textures that Lin, an artist, made turn to mosaic when zoomed in on the big screen. You split them into three levels of detail, sharper the closer you get, and in the command center the client zooms in again and again with the remote pointer.

An office building model from the design institute is missing a floor. You count against the CAD drawings three times and phone them. They say that floor was added later and the drawings were never updated.

Peng has you match the numbers of twenty robots in the hall to the models in the scene. You walk the floor all afternoon with the tag sheet and find two whose nameplates are swapped relative to the sheet.

A cold-storage client wants to see the temperature of every bay. You install a gateway on site, bring forty temperature channels into the time-series database over MQTT, and color every bay above minus fifteen orange in the scene.

The line equipment vendor's engineer says their PLC doesn't open its data. You don't argue; you ask whether you could read just three registers. He thinks it over and agrees, and those three numbers are just enough for a line-stop alarm.

On acceptance day the client's IT section chief ticks items off in front of the big screen. He asks why one air compressor's data is gray. You say it's down for maintenance these two days and really isn't running on site. He signs the acceptance form.

You build a cycle-time simulation of a body welding line, and the slowest station turns out to be the manual touch-up welding at station seven. The plant's process engineer doesn't believe it, spends the next morning on the floor with a stopwatch, and comes back to say you're right.

A vibration prediction model for a fan keeps alarming too early. You and a researcher from a university go through three months of data and find the baseline differs between summer and winter, so you add the season to the model.

The client's technical section chief asks why he should believe the simulation's eight percent output gain. You spread out the virtual-versus-real error table and go through it row by row until he runs out of questions.

On a development zone project, the client's wish list fills three pages. You sit with their department director for an afternoon and cut it to one page: phase one covers only the park's energy use. He agrees.

Two people on your team argue all the way up to you over which engine to use. You don't take sides. You have each build a small prototype and run it on the same old client computer; whichever doesn't stutter wins.

A city platform company's final payment is a year overdue. Once a month you go sit in their office with the acceptance form and the maintenance records. On the eleventh visit, finance says the money goes out next week.

Chairing the architecture review for the new platform, you hear a team lead propose delivering AI-generated scenes as is. You add a line to the review form: every connected data point must be checked and signed for by someone on site.

A carmaker's technical head comes to discuss a three-year framework deal. You don't talk about visuals; you talk about how much of the data from their twenty shops can actually be connected today, and he extends the meeting by an hour.
In the annual technical plan you cut a flashy big-screen effects module two years in the making, with the reason on the first line: clients no longer pay for pretty.
past: You go to middle school in Xiangyang and get hooked on a game where you can build your own maps. On weekends in an internet cafe you build your school block by block, down to the crooked tree beside the sports field.

Your gaokao (college entrance exam) score is enough for an engineering university in Wuhan. You want game design; your father says that's not a proper job. In the end you meet halfway and put down automation.
In your first year PLC classes put you to sleep, but in a student club you use Unity to build a little campus tour app, and the admissions office uses it for a year.

In your third year you enter a robotics competition, building a 3D model of the robot in the computer so it can practice in a virtual arena first. You win second prize, and realize you prefer the robot in the computer.

In your senior year you intern at a company in Optics Valley and walk into a district command hall for the first time, where the whole district moves across a screen dozens of meters long. At the end of the internship your supervisor says if you want to come after graduation, just call him. You call.

late.pension_note: Estimate: private software companies in Wuhan mostly pay pension contributions on a lower-to-middling share of actual wages, with no company annuity, so the basic pension comes to a little under half your last monthly pay.
scenes: In your first month of retirement you still wake at 8:30, go downstairs for a bowl of hot dry noodles, and only after finishing it remember there's no bus to catch.
Your old company brings you back as an adviser once a quarter, only for technical reviews. On a young engineer's plan you write: have you been to the site to look at this data feed?
You make a 3D map of the residential compound for the seniors' activity center, every building and entrance at a glance. The delivery riders say it's much easier to find their way now.
Your grandchild, headset on, flies around a virtual city and asks if you used to make this. You say more or less, except back then the buildings had to be placed one by one.
In the first days after you stop, you sit by East Lake every morning watching the water slowly brighten, and your eyes stop aching.
Your back improves, and you start cycling with people from the neighborhood, from East Lake to the Yangtze, watching the boats on the river go by one after another.
On the day you file your retirement papers you pass the district command center; the sign at the door has a new name. You don't go in. You stand across the street a while, looking at that window.
In the first year on a different road, whenever you walk into any factory building your eyes still go first to the sensors and gateways on the walls.

Back in Optics Valley on an errand, you see your old company's building now bears another company's name. The hot dry noodle vendor downstairs still recognizes you and asks where you've been all this time.
An implementation engineer you trained has become head of R&D. He sends you a photo: the old hard hat from the shop floor gate, which he has kept on his office bookshelf all along.
Wuhan has built several more metro lines. Sitting in the carriage studying the route map, your mind turns it into a 3D model on its own, every station clear down to how many levels underground it is.

On an old hard drive you find the project files for the first city screen. It takes ages to open; the river's transparent material is still there, and the moment you turn the camera it stutters. You watch it stutter for a while, and laugh.

closing.retire: Many years later, one evening, you stand on the Yangtze River Bridge watching the lights come on along both banks. You know that on some screen you can't see, this bridge is lit up too, every hanger cable moving ever so slightly.
closing.burnout: Many years later, you are watering plants on the balcony when it starts to rain. You think of the waterlogging module, of the red dots lighting up one by one on the screen, watch the rain a while longer, and close the window.
closing.end: Many years later, in a drawer, you find the tag sheet from your first time on site, the paper gone yellow, two numbers on it corrected in Peng's red pen. You look at it a while, fold it, and put it back where it was.
